lead: You'll write the brief for a small tool that joins two sources of work information, and Cowork will turn it into a one-page plan you build from for the rest of this level. The example is a customer issue tracker, but you can pick any tool your team would use. The bracketed parts are decisions only you can make.
why: A plan with a clear acceptance test keeps a build with many parts on track, and the later missions in this level read from it.
result: A one-page product plan, product-plan.md, with a testable definition of done, saved in your Cowork Academy folder.

think.scene: At work: a hospital group's finance team spends every Friday matching supplier invoices in one system against purchase orders in another.
think.ask: Which two systems do people at your company bridge by hand?

steps.title: Write the brief
steps.do: Replace every bracketed part with your own decision. Then paste it into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: I'm planning a small internal tool for my team at [your company and team, e.g. a law firm's client intake team]. Problem: [the problem in one sentence]. Users: [who uses it, and when]. Sources: [two sources, e.g. support-tickets.csv and customer-feedback.csv]. Done means: [a test you could check, e.g. a manager sees which customers have unresolved issues in under a minute]. Ask me up to 4 questions about anything unclear, one at a time.
steps.see: Cowork asks you a single question, such as how often the users would open the tool or what they do today instead.
steps.stuck: No idea yet? Use the example: a customer issue tracker that combines support-tickets.csv and customer-feedback.csv for Lakeview Supply Co. Both files are already in your Cowork Academy folder. If Cowork writes a plan straight away, reply: 'Stop. Ask me your questions first, one at a time.'

steps.title: Answer, then save the plan
steps.do: Answer each question in a sentence or two. After the last one, fill in the brackets below, paste it into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Write a one-page plan and save it in this folder as product-plan.md. Sections: problem and users, the done test, data sources, the pages of a small internal website, one job I'd delegate: [e.g. a weekly review of low-rated feedback], one task to save as a skill: [e.g. replying to a customer complaint in our voice], and open questions.
steps.see: product-plan.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with a short section for each item, including your done test word for word.
steps.stuck: If a section is vague, such as 'a messaging app', reply: 'Name the exact source for each section and update product-plan.md.'

steps.title: Pressure-test it
steps.do: Fill in the bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read product-plan.md as a skeptical [who will judge it, e.g. our head of operations, or the finance director]. Does every section serve the done test? List up to 3 gaps, and suggest one thing to cut. Update the file only after I agree.
steps.see: Up to three specific gaps and one suggested cut. After you agree, Cowork updates product-plan.md.
steps.stuck: If Cowork says the plan is fine, ask: 'Which section would fail first if we built it tomorrow?'

steps.q: You draft your brief and the done test says: 'The tool looks good and the team likes it.' What should you change before you build?
options: Keep it open so the plan can change as you build
Rewrite it as something you can check, like a time
Add more pages so there's more for the team to like
steps.why: A done test must be something you can pass or fail, such as 'a manager finds the top issue in under a minute'. An open test sounds flexible, but you can never tell whether the build succeeded.

lead: You'll have Cowork build a small internal website from your plan, then review it from your users' point of view. At this level you write the brief: you decide the pages and what the site must let people do.
why: A clear, accessible internal page gets used. A confusing one gets ignored.
result: A multi-page internal website in a site folder, reviewed for design, wording and accessibility against your own done test.

think.scene: At work: a school district's front office bookmarks one clear page showing which families still owe forms, and ignores the old shared drive.
think.ask: What internal page would people actually bookmark?

steps.title: Build the site
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read product-plan.md (or sample-business-brief.md if you don't have one). Build the internal website it describes as linked HTML pages in a new folder called site: [the pages, e.g. a home page, an open issues page and an issues by customer page]. It must [your done test, e.g. let a manager find any customer's open issues in two clicks] and work at phone width. Use sample data from the practice files.
steps.see: A folder called site appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with index.html and the other pages you asked for.
steps.stuck: Don't have product-plan.md? The prompt falls back to sample-business-brief.md, which is already in your folder. If neither is there, describe your tool in two sentences at the start of the prompt.

steps.title: Test it yourself
steps.do: Open index.html from the site folder in your Cowork Academy folder. Click every link, then try your done test as if you were one of your users.
steps.see: The site opens in your web browser, every link works, and you can tell whether your done test passes.
steps.stuck: If it opens as code in a text editor, right-click index.html and choose to open it with your web browser.

steps.title: Review and fix
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Review the site as [your user, e.g. a support agent checking it on a phone between calls, or a store manager on the shop floor]. Do a design critique, a plain-language pass and an accessibility check (contrast, text size, tap targets). List the top 3 issues in each, fix them, and confirm the site still passes: [your done test]. Also fix this, which I found: [one thing that bothered you].
steps.see: Three short lists of issues, a summary of what Cowork changed, and a line on whether the done test still passes. Refresh the page in your browser to see the fixes.
steps.stuck: If the fixes don't show, refresh the browser page. If the site still feels like a first draft, ask: 'Do a second, tighter design pass, and show me what you changed.'

steps.q: The first draft looks fine on your laptop. Your users are warehouse supervisors who check it on a phone while walking the floor. What do you do next?
options: Review it at phone width as they would, then fix it
Send them the link and gather their feedback next week
Ask for a few new designs and pick the nicest one
steps.why: The people who use it decide whether it works, and they use a phone. Checking at that size first catches problems before your users do. Waiting a week for feedback wastes their first impression.

t: Delegate a job and build a skill
lead: You'll write a delegation brief for a self-contained job, judge what comes back, then save a repeatable task as a custom skill. The goal, scope, sources and output format are yours to decide.
why: A clear brief is how you hand off a big job, whoever or whatever does it, and a skill lets you repeat a task the same way every time.
result: agent-result.md from your own delegation brief, and a saved custom skill tested in a new task.

think.scene: At work: a recruiter's assistant researches every shortlisted candidate's public work history, and a saved skill drafts the first message in the company's tone.
think.ask: Which multi-step process could split into a research part and a draft part?

steps.title: Write the brief
steps.do: Fill in all four parts of the brief: goal, scope, sources and output format. Then paste it into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt:
Treat this as a delegated job and follow the brief exactly.
Goal: [the decision this helps, e.g. which region the sales director should call first].
Scope: [what's in and out, e.g. responses from July to September 2026, no contact with customers].
Sources: customer-feedback.csv and [any other file, or none].
Output format: [e.g. a ranked table of the 3 lowest-rated customers with the comments behind each].
Save the result as agent-result.md.
steps.see: Cowork works through the job, then agent-result.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder in the format you asked for.
steps.stuck: Cowork may do the job in this task or hand it to a helper, depending on your setup. Either is fine: you're practicing the brief. If the result misses, change the brief part that caused it and run it again.

steps.title: Judge the output
steps.do: Open agent-result.md and compare it with your four brief parts. Then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Check agent-result.md against my brief, part by part: goal, scope, sources and output format. Say where it falls short, and show me how you got the two most important numbers so I can check them in customer-feedback.csv.
steps.see: A part-by-part check against your brief, and the working behind two numbers, such as a customer's average rating and how many responses it's based on.
steps.stuck: If the working doesn't match the file, ask: 'Recalculate that from customer-feedback.csv and show me the rows you used.'

steps.title: Build the skill
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Create a custom skill for a task I repeat: [the task, e.g. replying to a customer complaint in our voice, or summarizing a supplier call for the finance team]. Good output means: [your criteria, e.g. under 120 words, apologizes once, offers one concrete fix, promises no refunds]. Ask me for one real-looking example before you write it.
steps.see: Cowork asks for an example, then creates the skill. It may ask you to approve the skill or turn it on.
steps.stuck: If Cowork asks you to approve or turn on the skill, do it. If you can't find where, check Claude's help center at support.claude.com, or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.title: Test it in a new task
steps.do: Start a new Cowork task in your Cowork Academy folder. Fill in the bracket, then paste this and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Use my [skill name] skill on the lowest-rated comment in agent-result.md (or in customer-feedback.csv if you don't have that file). Save the output as skill-test.md, and tell me which of the skill's criteria it met.
steps.see: skill-test.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, written to your criteria, with a note on which ones it met.
steps.stuck: If Cowork doesn't seem to know the skill, check that you approved it or turned it on, then name the skill again in your request.

steps.q: Your brief asked for the 3 lowest-rated customers, but agent-result.md ranks all 30 in a long essay. Which part of the brief should you change?
options: The goal, so it asks for a full customer review
The output format, with a set count and layout
Nothing, since extra detail gives you more to use
steps.why: The goal was fine. The format was loose, so the result came back long and unfocused. Naming a count and a layout, like a ranked table of 3, fixes it. Widening the goal would make the output longer still.

lead: You'll have Cowork read two sources of work information and match them up into drafts, for example customer messages checked against open support tickets. You decide what starts the workflow, what gets matched and what the drafts say.
why: A lot of manual work is moving information from one place to another. With both sources in reach, Cowork can do the bridging and you approve the result.
result: bridge-drafts.md: drafts that combine information from two sources, with nothing sent, changed or deleted.

think.scene: At work: when a sales coordinator marks a contract as signed in the CRM, an onboarding task and a welcome email draft should appear without retyping.
think.ask: Where does information arrive in one place and then need to go somewhere else?

steps.title: Pick your two sources
steps.do: Only connect apps your company has approved, and sign in yourself in any pop-up. Then fill in the brackets, paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Show me one small sample from each of these two sources so I know both work: [source 1, e.g. customer-messages.txt or my company calendar] and [source 2, e.g. support-tickets.csv or a shared team sheet]. Don't send, change or delete anything.
steps.see: A short sample from each source, for example two customer messages and the first few rows of the tickets.
steps.stuck: Use a real inbox or calendar only if your company has approved this connector. Otherwise, use customer-messages.txt and support-tickets.csv, which are already in your folder. For help connecting an approved app, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.title: Brief the workflow
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Build one workflow from these two sources. Starts when: [the trigger, e.g. a customer message mentions an invoice or a delivery problem]. From source 1, take: [e.g. the customer and the problem]. Match it in source 2 with: [e.g. open tickets for that customer]. Each draft must: [your criteria, e.g. give the customer a realistic next step and name the ticket]. Save all drafts in this folder as bridge-drafts.md. Don't send, change or delete anything.
steps.see: bridge-drafts.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with one draft per matched item that names details from both sources.
steps.stuck: If Cowork starts to send or change something, reply: 'Stop. Drafts in bridge-drafts.md only.' Then check the app to see whether anything changed.

steps.title: Check two drafts
steps.do: Open bridge-drafts.md. Pick two drafts and check each one against the original item in both sources.
steps.see: Each draft you checked names the right item from source 1 and the right match from source 2.
steps.stuck: If a draft matched the wrong item, tell Cowork which one and why, and ask it to tighten the matching rule and redo bridge-drafts.md.

steps.q: Your workflow matches customer messages to support tickets and saves drafts. One draft tells a customer their invoice copy was sent, but ticket CS-1204 is still Open. What do you do?
options: Close the ticket so the two sources agree again
Send it anyway, since the customer will flag any issue
Fix the draft, then tighten the matching rule
steps.why: The ticket is the record of what's true, so the draft is wrong. Fixing the draft and the rule that produced it stops the same error repeating. Closing the ticket would hide the problem.

lead: You'll build a dashboard from the support ticket and customer feedback data, with 4 or 5 signals and a 'what changed' summary, and learn to refresh it by rebuilding. You decide who reads it and what decision each signal supports.
why: A dashboard you can rebuild in one paste can replace a meeting that exists only to share numbers.
result: dashboard.html with 4 or 5 decision-led signals, plus refresh.md, a saved prompt that rebuilds it from the newest data.

think.scene: At work: a hospital facilities team replaces its Monday status meeting with a one-page 'what changed and why' summary.
think.ask: Which meeting exists only to share numbers?

steps.title: Pick the signals
steps.do: support-tickets.csv and customer-feedback.csv are already in your Cowork Academy folder. Fill in the brackets, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read product-plan.md (or sample-business-brief.md if you don't have one). Using support-tickets.csv and customer-feedback.csv, propose 4 or 5 signals for a dashboard read by [who, e.g. the Monday customer service meeting]. Each signal must help decide [the decision, e.g. which region or ticket category needs action this week]. Include the number of Delivery tickets opened each month. Drop any signal that doesn't lead to a decision.
steps.see: A short list of signals, each with the decision it supports, such as 'Average rating by region: where to send help first.'
steps.stuck: If a signal has no clear decision, reply: 'Replace that one with a signal someone would act on this week.'

steps.title: Build it
steps.do: Fill in the bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter. Open dashboard.html from your folder when it's ready.
steps.prompt: Build those signals as dashboard.html in this folder, one tile each, with a 'what changed' summary at the top comparing September 2026 with August 2026. It must pass this test: [your done test, e.g. a manager can name the top problem in 30 seconds]. Also save refresh.md with the exact prompt I can paste to rebuild it from the newest data.
steps.see: dashboard.html opens in your browser with a tile per signal and a short summary at the top. refresh.md is in your folder.
steps.stuck: If dashboard.html opens as code, right-click it and choose to open it with your web browser. The file doesn't update by itself: you refresh it by asking Cowork to rebuild it.

steps.title: Test a refresh
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. Coming back later with newer data to use refresh.md is optional.
steps.prompt: Copy support-tickets.csv to tickets-test.csv and add one Open Delivery ticket for Desert Bloom Clinics in the West, opened 2026-09-30. Rebuild the dashboard from tickets-test.csv as dashboard-test.html, and tell me which tiles changed.
steps.see: dashboard-test.html appears in your folder, and Cowork names the tiles that changed, such as the open ticket count or West Delivery tickets.
steps.stuck: If Cowork edits support-tickets.csv itself, ask it to undo that change. Other missions rely on the original file.

steps.q: Your 'what changed' summary compares Delivery tickets opened in September 2026 with August 2026. What does it show?
options: It fell from 15 to 9
It fell from 15 to 10
It rose from 9 to 10
steps.why: August had 9 Delivery tickets and September had 10. The 15 is July, so the two falling answers compare the wrong months.

t: Automate the web with Claude in Chrome
lead: You'll have Cowork use your web browser to collect information for your tool from a site with no export button. You decide the site, what to collect and how you'll know it's right.
why: Optional: this needs the Claude in Chrome browser extension, which may not be available to you. When it works, it ends copying information out of websites by hand.
result: web-results.md, collected by Cowork in your browser and spot-checked by you.

think.scene: At work: nobody at a regional bank copies exchange rates or competitor fee schedules from public web pages into a spreadsheet by hand anymore.
think.ask: Which website do you copy information from by hand?

steps.title: Check it's available
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Can you use my Chrome browser through Claude in Chrome in this task right now? Answer yes or no, and don't change any settings.
steps.see: A clear yes or no.
steps.stuck: If the answer is no, or your company doesn't allow browser extensions, skip this mission. Nothing later in this level depends on it. For setup help, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.title: Brief the web task
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter. If the site asks you to sign in, do it yourself.
steps.prompt: Using Claude in Chrome, go to [a site you use for work, e.g. a supplier's price list, a public tender portal or a carrier's tracking page]. Collect [what you need, e.g. prices for our 5 most-ordered items]. Done means: [your test, e.g. every item has a price, a unit size and the page it came from]. Don't buy, submit or send anything. Save it in this folder as web-results.md.
steps.see: Chrome moves through the site while Cowork reports what it's doing. Then web-results.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder.
steps.stuck: If Cowork asks to submit, buy or send something, say no. If the site blocks it, try a public page with the same kind of information.

steps.title: Spot-check the results
steps.do: Pick two items in web-results.md and compare them with the website yourself.
steps.see: Both items match what the site shows today, and each one meets your done test.
steps.stuck: If something doesn't match, reply: 'The entry for [item] doesn't match the site. Check it again and show me where you found it.'

steps.q: Cowork has collected supplier prices and reaches an order form with a Submit button. What should happen next?
options: Cowork submits, since the prices were checked
Cowork stops, and you decide about submitting
Cowork submits a small test order to try it
steps.why: Collecting information is safe to hand over. Spending money or sending a form is your decision, and you set that limit in the brief. A small test order is still a real order.

lead: You'll have Cowork control a desktop app on your computer, clicking and typing, to do one small, reversible task. You pick the task and the test for whether it worked.
why: Optional: computer control depends on your setup and may not be available to you. When it works, it handles tasks in apps that have no connector.
result: One small, reversible task done by Cowork in a desktop app, checked by you.

think.scene: At work: a law firm's records clerk has Cowork rename, sort and file hundreds of scanned case documents in minutes.
think.ask: What file or folder cleanup keeps getting put off?

steps.title: Check it's available
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Can you control desktop apps on my computer in this task right now? Answer yes or no, and if yes, name the kinds of apps.
steps.see: A clear yes or no, and if yes, the kinds of apps it can use.
steps.stuck: If the answer is no, or your company has computer control turned off, skip this mission. Nothing later in this level depends on it. For setup help, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.title: Brief a small task
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into the same task and press Enter. Read any permission request before you allow it.
steps.prompt: Do one small, reversible task in a desktop app: [the task, e.g. open a text editor and draft a launch checklist from product-plan.md]. Done means: [your test, e.g. a saved file with 8 to 10 checklist items]. Don't delete, send or pay for anything. Tell me exactly what you did.
steps.see: The app opens and you watch Cowork click and type in it, followed by a short report of what it did.
steps.stuck: If you're not comfortable with what a permission request allows, deny it and pick a smaller task. Don't have product-plan.md? Use sample-business-brief.md instead.

steps.title: Check the result
steps.do: Open the app yourself and look at what Cowork made or changed.
steps.see: The work is there, matches Cowork's report and passes your done test.
steps.stuck: If anything looks wrong, undo it in the app yourself, then tell Cowork what went wrong.

steps.q: Computer control works for you, and you want to try it on real work. Which task should you start with?
options: Clearing out last year's old order exports
Sending the weekly customer updates from your email
Drafting a checklist in a new text file
steps.why: A new file can be thrown away if it goes wrong. Deleting files or sending messages can't be undone, so those need much more trust built first.

lead: You'll see which plugins you can use, check what one adds before installing it, and use it on a task for your tool. You decide the task and what good output looks like.
why: Optional: plugins may not be available in your setup. When they are, a plugin adds a set of skills and connectors at once, so a team gets a ready-made toolkit.
result: One installed plugin and a piece of work made with it that meets your own criteria.

think.scene: At work: a finance or sales plugin gives a team a ready-made toolkit for its specialty, such as month-end close checklists or call preparation.
think.ask: Which department would benefit most from a ready-made toolkit?

steps.title: See what's available
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Which plugins can you see that are installed or available to me right now? List only ones you can actually see, with one line on what each adds. If you can't see any, say so.
steps.see: A short list of plugins with what each adds, or a clear statement that none are visible.
steps.stuck: If none are available, or your company limits plugins, skip this mission. Nothing later in this level depends on it. To learn where plugins are installed, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.title: Vet it, then install
steps.do: Fill in the bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter. Install it only if what it can access is fine for your work.
steps.prompt: Before I install [a plugin from the list], tell me what it adds and what apps or data it can access. Then tell me whether it fits product-plan.md (or sample-business-brief.md).
steps.see: A short explanation of what the plugin adds and what it can reach. Once you install it, Cowork may ask you to approve or turn it on.
steps.stuck: If it asks you to sign in to an app, do it yourself, and only for apps your company has approved. If your account can't install plugins, use one that's already installed.

steps.title: Use it
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Use [the plugin] on this task: [the task, e.g. a weekly summary of support-tickets.csv for the customer success team]. Good output means: [your criteria, e.g. one page, top 3 problem categories, no internal jargon]. Tell me which skill or tool from the plugin you used, and which criteria the output met.
steps.see: Finished work, plus a note naming the plugin skill or tool Cowork used and how it scored against your criteria.
steps.stuck: If Cowork does the work without the plugin, reply: 'Redo this using the plugin, and name the skill you used.'

steps.q: A teammate shares a plugin that adds a reporting skill and an email connector. Before you install it, what should you check first?
options: How many skills it adds compared with others
What it can access, and whether that's approved
Whether your teammate has used it for a while
steps.why: A plugin can reach your files and apps, so access and approval come first. Skill counts and a colleague's experience don't tell you whether it's safe to use with company data.

lead: You'll chain a data source, your custom skill and a delegated job into one workflow, test it once, then put it on a schedule. You design the chain and its done test.
why: This is the difference between using Cowork and building with it: the work runs as a set process, and you review the results.
result: workflow.md, a chain of a source, a skill and a delegated job, with one test run checked by you and a schedule or on-demand plan.

think.scene: At work: an insurance claims team has new claims sorted and summarized overnight, so adjusters review the results first thing in the morning.
think.ask: Which process would you trust to run overnight if you could check the result first?

steps.title: Design the chain
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read product-plan.md (or sample-business-brief.md). Design one workflow. Input: [a source, e.g. support-tickets.csv or an approved app]. Delegated job: [goal, scope and output format, e.g. rank open tickets by customer impact in a table]. Skill: use my [skill name] skill to [what it does, e.g. draft status updates for the top 3 customers]. Done means: [your test]. Outbound stays a draft. Save numbered steps as workflow.md.
steps.see: workflow.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder, with numbered steps naming the input, the delegated job, the skill and your done test.
steps.stuck: No custom skill yet? Replace the skill line with two or three written rules, such as 'under 100 words, plain English'. Don't have product-plan.md? The prompt falls back to sample-business-brief.md.

steps.title: Test it once
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Run workflow.md once now, step by step. Show me what each step produced and where it handed off to the next, then tell me whether the run passed my done test.
steps.see: A run-through of each step and its output, ending with drafts for you to review and a pass or fail against your test.
steps.stuck: If one step fails, fix it on its own first. Reply: 'Run only step [number] and show me what goes wrong.'

steps.title: Put it on a schedule
steps.do: Fill in the bracket, then paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Schedule workflow.md to run [how often, e.g. every Monday at 8am]. Save results in this folder and keep anything outbound as drafts. Tell me the schedule's name and when it runs next.
steps.see: Cowork confirms the schedule's name and the next run time.
steps.stuck: Scheduled tasks may only run while your computer is on and the Claude app is open. If scheduling isn't available, run it on demand by pasting 'Run workflow.md once now.' To pause or delete a schedule, check support.claude.com or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.q: Monday's scheduled run of workflow.md saved drafts, but the ranking step left out two of the 7 open tickets. What's the best fix?
options: Run that step alone, fix it, then rerun
Rebuild workflow.md from a fresh brief
Add a check step at the end of the chain
steps.why: The fault is in one step, so isolate it, fix it and rerun the chain. Starting over throws away the parts that work, and an extra check at the end doesn't repair the ranking.

lead: You'll tell Cowork what you built, get a 5-minute demo script, then find the weakest part and save a launch summary. You name the audience and the parts you finished.
why: Being able to explain how each piece works is what makes you the person colleagues come to for help with AI.
result: demo-script.md and launch-summary.md, saved in your Cowork Academy folder.

think.scene: At work: the analyst who can explain how the monthly sales report is built becomes the company's go-to AI champion.
think.ask: Who would you demo this to, and which of their problems would it solve?

steps.title: Write the demo script
steps.do: Fill in every bracket, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Here's what I built: [the parts you finished, e.g. the site folder, dashboard.html, a complaint-reply skill, workflow.md]. List the files in this folder to confirm. Then write a 5-minute demo for [your audience, e.g. my department head, or the finance team] showing how it meets: [your done test from product-plan.md]. Name the Cowork feature behind each part. Save it as demo-script.md.
steps.see: A list of the files in your folder, then demo-script.md appears, split into timed sections with the feature behind each part.
steps.stuck: Cowork can't see skills or connectors from earlier tasks, so name them yourself in the prompt. If you skipped missions, list only what you finished. Don't have product-plan.md? Write your done test in one sentence instead.

steps.title: Find the weak spot and save
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: What's the single weakest part of this product, and what one change would improve it most? Then save a one-page launch-summary.md: what it does, who it helps, what's built, the weak spot and its fix, and 3 ideas for a next version.
steps.see: One named weak spot with a concrete fix, then launch-summary.md appears in your Cowork Academy folder with those sections.
steps.stuck: If Cowork lists several weak spots, reply: 'Pick only the one that matters most, and update launch-summary.md.'

steps.q: During your demo, a director asks why the dashboard's numbers differ from last week's. What shows you really understand the tool?
options: Saying that Cowork built it, so you'd ask it
Explaining that it's rebuilt from the newest data
Promising to look into it after the meeting
steps.why: The dashboard is a file that's rebuilt from whatever data is current, so changed numbers usually mean changed data. Knowing that lets you answer on the spot instead of deferring.

lead: You'll check your site folder for anything private, then publish it to a web address you can share. You decide who it's for and what must stay off it.
why: Optional: skip it if your company doesn't allow public sites or you'd rather keep your work in your folder. Publishing usually takes 30 minutes or more the first time.
result: Your product site, checked for private data and published at a shareable web address.

think.scene: At work: a nonprofit's program team shares one link so partner agencies can use the intake tool they built.
think.ask: Who should see what you built, and what would you ask them?

steps.title: Check it's safe to share
steps.do: Fill in the brackets, then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Before I publish the site folder for [who will see it, e.g. anyone with the link], check every file. List anything private: customer or employee names, emails, phone numbers, passwords, internal figures and [anything else that must stay off, e.g. supplier prices or salaries]. Suggest a safe replacement for each, and change the files only after I agree.
steps.see: A list of private items with a suggested fix for each, or a clear note that nothing private was found.
steps.stuck: Don't have a site folder? Skip this mission, or do 'Build the multi-page website' first. If the site includes a dashboard built from real company data, ask: 'Remove the dashboard from the version I publish.'

steps.title: Publish it
steps.do: If your company has an approved place for internal pages, use it and stop here. Otherwise, paste this into the same task, press Enter and follow each step.
steps.prompt: Walk me through publishing the site folder to a free host such as GitHub Pages, one step at a time. Wait for me to finish each step before you give the next one. I'll create any accounts and sign in myself.
steps.see: Only the first step, for example creating a GitHub account, then Cowork waits. At the end you have a web address, and every page loads there on your computer and your phone.
steps.stuck: Check your company's rules about public websites before you publish. A new site can take a few minutes to appear. If a page shows a 404 error, tell Cowork which page and ask it to find the cause.

steps.q: Your site includes a dashboard built from your company's real customer ticket export. You're about to publish to a public address. What do you do?
options: Publish it, since the address is hard to guess
Publish it, but only share the link with your team
Swap in practice data, or leave it off
steps.why: Anyone who finds a public address can read it, and a link shared with a team can be forwarded. Real customer data should not be on a public site at all.
